readerTitle: The store that added 2,000 products and lost its best customers
caseNote: 가상 사례 (건축자재 유통점, 금속 부품 제조사) · 모든 상황과 수치는 설명용
insight: 고객이 떠나는 이유는 제품 안보다 제품 주변(배송, 대기, 서류, 반품)의 고통에 있는 경우가 많다. 고통과 이득을 빈도와 비용으로 순위를 매겨야 무엇을 고칠지 보인다.
misconception: 고객을 붙잡으려면 상품과 기능, 즉 얻는 것(이득)을 더 늘리면 된다.

sources.text: Osterwalder, A., Pigneur, Y., Bernarda, G., & Smith, A. (2014). Value Proposition Design. Wiley. (customer pains and gains)
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Pains/gains 구분은 Osterwalder 외(2014) Value Proposition Design의 고객 프로필 개념을 따릅니다. 4번 카드에는 출처 이름을 넣지 않고 원리만 설명했습니다. 정의 문구가 원전과 크게 어긋나지 않는지 확인하세요.
건축자재점(2,000개 상품, 4시간 배송 창, 4인 작업팀)과 브래킷 제조사(3% 할인, 반나절 라인 정지)는 모두 가상 수치입니다. 실제 통계처럼 읽히지 않는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: The store that added 2,000 products and lost its best customers
body: A building-supply store added 2,000 new products, a bright showroom and a loyalty card.
Within a year, several of its biggest contractor accounts had moved to a rival with a smaller range and a plain warehouse. The rival wasn't cheaper either.

image.label: Bright showroom on one side, plain warehouse with a loaded truck on the other
image.brief: 화면을 좌우로 나눔. 왼쪽은 진열대가 가득하고 조명이 화려한 매장인데 손님이 없음. 오른쪽은 소박한 창고 앞에서 작업복 차림 고객들이 트럭에 짐을 싣고 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고나 간판 없음.

cards.title: You own the store. What do you do first?
body: Your contractors aren't complaining. They're just ordering less, and some have stopped ordering at all.
You have time for one move this month.

options.text: Survey contractors on which new products and services they value most
options.feedback: You'll learn which of your additions people like. But the questions only cover what's inside your store, and the reason they left may sit outside it.

options.text: Follow a few orders from phone call to job site and note what goes wrong
options.feedback: Slower than a survey, but you see the whole job as the customer lives it, including the parts you never think about.

options.text: Cut prices on your top sellers to match the rival
options.feedback: The rival isn't cheaper, so price probably isn't the reason. You'd give up margin to fix a problem you may not have.

cards.title: The problem wasn't on the shelves.
body: Following the orders, the owner saw it. Deliveries came in a four-hour window, so a crew of four often stood waiting. About one order in several arrived with something missing. One missing box of screws could stall a job for half a day.
The rival checked every order against a list before loading and texted 30 minutes before arrival. That was enough.

cards.title: Pains and gains
body: **Pains** are the costs, hassles and risks customers face while getting something done. **Gains** are the results and extras they hope for.

The store poured money into gains: more choice, a nicer showroom. The contractors' biggest pain, paid crews standing idle, went untouched. They weren't really buying screws. They were trying to finish jobs on time.

image.label: Scale with pains on one side and gains on the other
image.brief: 저울 일러스트. 한쪽 접시에는 "Pains" 라벨과 함께 기다리는 작업자, 빈 상자, 시계 아이콘이 무겁게 내려가 있음. 다른 쪽에는 "Gains" 라벨과 진열대, 별 아이콘이 가볍게 올라가 있음.

cards.softwareNote: Teams often ship new features (gains) while users quietly leave over pains around the product: a confusing setup, a broken import, an invoice finance can't read. Check your cancellation reasons before your feature list.

cards.title: Map the whole job, then rank.
body: Pains show up at every stage, not just when the product is in use:
list: **Before:** hard to order, unsure what's in stock
**After:** returns, invoices that don't match the order
cards.callout: For each pain, ask two things: how often does it happen, and what does it cost when it does? Fix the ones high on both.

cards.title: The worst pain often sits around the product.
body: A bakery can have the best bread in town and still lose customers to a 20-minute queue. A clinic can have great doctors and lose patients to a booking line that never answers.
Customers judge the whole experience of getting the job done. An excellent product with painful edges often loses to an ordinary one that's easy to buy, receive and use.

cards.title: Not every pain is worth fixing.
body: Ask customers about pains and you'll get a long list. Some are rare, some are mild, and some cost more to fix than they're worth. Ranking matters more than listing.
People also describe pains differently from how they act. Watch what they do, not just what they say.
And gains still count. Once every rival fixes the same pain, the extras decide who wins.

cards.title: Now you make metal parts.
body: You make brackets for a furniture factory. Its plant manager mentions that last month a batch arrived mixed with another order. Sorting it stopped one assembly line for a morning.
You have budget for one improvement this year.

options.text: Offer new powder-coat colors that buyers have said they like
options.feedback: A real gain, and it may win some new orders. But a nicer color doesn't prevent a stopped line, which is what this customer feels most.

options.text: Pack and label every batch by order and line, and confirm ship dates
options.feedback: It targets the pain that costs the customer the most. A morning of a stopped line likely costs them more than anything you could add.

options.text: Give a 3% discount next year to keep goodwill
options.feedback: It costs you margin every month while the real problem stays. One more mixed batch could cost them more than the whole discount.

cards.title: Find the pain that costs customers most, even if it's outside your product.
body: Adding gains feels like progress. But customers often leave over the hassle around the product, not the product itself.
**Try it today:** call one recent customer. Ask them to walk you through the last time buying from you went wrong, and what it cost them.
